## The counterexample

In $X = (0,1]$ take $x_n = 1/n$. Every term is in $X$.

**It is Cauchy.** Given $\eps > 0$ choose $N > 2/\eps$. For $m, n \ge N$,

$$|x_m - x_n| \le \tfrac1m + \tfrac1n < \tfrac{\eps}{2} + \tfrac{\eps}{2} = \eps.$$

**It does not converge in $X$.** Suppose $x_n \to L$ for some $L \in (0,1]$. Then $L > 0$, so take $\eps = L/2$. For all large $n$ we would need $|1/n - L| < L/2$, hence $1/n > L/2$, hence $n < 2/L$ — which fails for every large $n$. So no $L$ in $X$ works.

## What is actually going on

Nothing is wrong with the sequence. It is heading for $0$ perfectly well; $0$ has simply been deleted from the space. **Completeness is a property of the space, not of the sequence.**

The same sequence inside $\R$ converges, because $\R$ still contains the point it wants. Remove one point and the same sequence has nowhere to go.

## The other standard example

$\Q$ with the usual metric. Take the decimal truncations of $\sqrt2$: $1, 1.4, 1.41, 1.414, \dots$. Each is rational, the sequence is Cauchy, and the limit is irrational — so it does not converge *in $\Q$*. This one is the motivation for constructing $\R$ at all: $\R$ is, in a precise sense, $\Q$ with exactly the missing limits added.

## Why "Cauchy" is worth having as a separate word

The definition of Cauchy never mentions a limit, so you can check it without knowing what the answer is. That is the whole point: it is the condition that lets you say *this sequence is trying to converge* before you know whether there is anything for it to converge to.
